speaker_notes.note: These focus refs are quoted Dante read aloud by a student. Jiang's interpretive voice enters in segments 0313, 0315, 0317, and 0319.

claims.claim: Jiang identifies the 'man not born' in Beatrice's explanation as Adam.
The quoted passage says humanity lay sick in a great error for centuries until the Word of God descended and reunited sundered human nature to his person by eternal love.
Jiang says Adam's fall creates a schism between God and humanity, leaving people estranged, guilty, and unable even to ask for forgiveness correctly.
The quoted passage says human nature was originally good and pure but was banished from paradise after turning away from truth and its own life.

Jiang argues that humans are born good because God breathes a spark of life into them, but free will allows them to choose evil and compound that evil into a descending pattern they struggle to reverse.

The quoted passage says that measured by assumed human nature the cross is justly suffered, yet measured by the person who suffers it becomes the greatest wrong, and it poses the explicit question of why God chose precisely this path for redemption.
Jiang restates the theological problem as follows: an infinite God could have chosen many redemptive paths, so the punishment of an innocent Jesus appears unjust from the human point of view.
The quoted answer says this ordinance remains hidden from anyone whose intellect has not matured within the flame of love.

chronology_notes.note: Beatrice's logic moves in sequence from Adam's fall, to humanity's long illness and the incarnation, to the later question of why the crucifixion was the fitting redemptive path.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes the fall feel existential rather than legalistic: the real disaster is that humanity breaks with God so badly that it no longer even knows how to ask forgiveness.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we don't even know how to ask for forgiveness
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns original sin into a lived condition of estrangement and incapacity, not just a rule violation in the distant past.

signature_moments.moment: Evil is described as a snowball: one bad act gathers force into another until the person no longer knows the way back.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives Jiang's free-will account a memorable causal image that can recur later in the read and lens work.

signature_moments.moment: The class reaches the hard center of the atonement problem: if God is infinite, why does redemption require the suffering of the innocent rather than some other solution?
signature_moments.source_phrase: why God had precisely this pathway for our redemption
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's main argumentative hinge and the reason the preceding Roman history suddenly turns into metaphysical crisis.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice's first answer is not intellectual technique but transformed love: without a mind matured in love, the logic of redemption stays invisible.
signature_moments.source_phrase: intellect has not matured within the flame of love
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It previews Jiang's larger claim that certain truths are inaccessible to detached analysis alone.

glossary_terms.term: the man who was not born
glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang identifies this phrase from Beatrice's argument as Adam.
The force by which the Word of God unites sundered human nature back to his person in the quoted passage.
Beatrice's standard for the kind of matured intellect needed to grasp why redemption takes the path it does.
